doc.title: Jamey Aebersold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 26, 2022

title: Sonny Rollins, Gunther Schuller and Blue 7
summary: Schuller's analysis of Rollins's Blue 7 solo, Rollins's reaction, and Hal Galper's attitude.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I wonder how you would feel if someone transcribed a solo of yours and, well it’s hard to speculate — but I do recall that Sonny Rollins recorded that song “Blue 7” and Gunther Schuller picked it apart and kept, you know, look how Sonny is inverting what he played twelve measures ago and the whole thematic development thing, and what I read was that Sonny Rollins was very intimidated afterwards and felt like oh I shouldn’t do that anymore.

Oh. Now I didn’t hear that but what I heard was Sonny Rollins said he would never read another review by Gunther Schuller. And then later I read that Sonny got over that. But I got the magazine. I forget what was the name of it, that had that solo in there. And I can remember being in college, buying it at the bookstore and opened it up and there’s that solo I’ve listened to dozens of times. It’s a classic solo. It’s embedded in my brain you know. For me nowadays to play a solo and to bring out something four minutes later, after the drum solo that I played in the first or second solo, I measured up to Sonny © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

Rollins. I mean I’m not as great as Sonny but I did what Sonny did you know. Well I remember seeing that solo in the book thinking — my first thought was this is fantastic. Because Gunther Schuller did all the work and here it is you know. And I wondered what Sonny was going to think of that and of course he didn’t think much of it. He thought — he thinks like say Hal Galper thinks, and that is if you can hear it you can take it but I’m not going to give it to you. I’m not going to write it down for you. Kids at the camp. “Hal, how’d you do that? Did you record it?” “No. Well find somebody to record it and take it off. I’m not going to tell you.” You know there’s that wall between [da-da-da-da- da-da] But Sonny Rollins was a classic and that record, CD, I still have out in my van. And I’m going to listen to it Wednesday on the way down to Bowling Green, Kentucky. And that “Blue 7” solo is fantastic. And the Max Roach and Doug Watkins and Tommy Flanagan I think on piano. That record made a big impression on me.
